newsitem.title: UK: Coated aspirin may not protect stomach - study.
newsitem.headline: Coated aspirin may not protect stomach - study.

text.p: Sugar-coating aspirin or otherwise buffering it may not stop it from irritating the stomach and causing bleeding, U.S. doctors reported on Friday.

Although buffered aspirin often costs more, it may not be any safer, Judith Kelly and colleagues at Boston University's School of Public Health said in a study published in the Lancet medical journal.
Aspirin is known to cause gastric bleeding, which is why some companies have tried coating tablets with silicon or cellulose, or buffering it with substances such as chalk.
Kelly's group checked to see whether this does any good. They studied the cases of 550 patients who had suffered serious bleeding and 1,200 who had not.
They found all types of aspirin increased the risk of bleeding by about three-fold. Doses of above 325 mg -- about one extra-strength aspirin tablet -- increased the risk six times.
"The assumption that these formulations are less harmful than plain aspirin may be mistaken," they wrote.
"At lower doses, which we defined as 325 mg or less, the risk was a threefold increase regardless of what formulation was taken," Kelly said in a telephone interview.
Kelly, an epidemiologist, said the overall risk of serious bleeding from taking aspirin was fairly high -- about 19 cases per 100,000 per year.
"What we are talking about here is major intestinal bleeding, which is vomiting blood or passing blood, which necessitates hospitalisation," she said.

"If you took 100,000 aspirin users about 19 of those per year would get gastrointestinal bleeding because they are taking aspirin. This is not new, but taking buffered aspirin does not reduce that risk."
Regular aspirin users were defined as those who took at least one tablet every other day.

There were two reasons why aspirin caused bleeding, she said. One is that is irritates the stomach lining. Another is that it inhibits blood clotting -- which, of course, increases the risk of bleeding and coating would not affect this.
In a commentary on the findings, Dr Deborah Symmons, an epidemiologist at the University of Manchester, noted that many people do not need to take such high doses of aspirin.
As little as 75 mg a day -- a quarter of a tablet -- will provide some of aspirin's many benefits, including preventing blood clots that can cause heart attacks and stroke.
But Kelly noted 75 mg was not enough to relieve a headache.
